questions.stem: As per Conservation International's current classification, how many Biodiversity Hotspots are officially recognized across the globe?

options.option_text: 25 globally recognized hotspot regions
34 globally recognized hotspot regions
36 globally recognized hotspot regions
42 globally recognized hotspot regions

questions.explanation: Conservation International currently recognizes 36 Biodiversity Hotspots worldwide, covering about 2.4% of Earth's land surface but supporting more than half its plant and vertebrate species. 34 is a common wrong recall from an earlier count before the 2011–2016 updates added new hotspots; 25 predates the major expansions of the concept.

questions.stem: Which of the following practices is correctly classified as an 'Ex-situ' conservation method?

options.option_text: Establishing wildlife sanctuaries with legal protection
Maintaining national parks with minimal human interference
Operating cryogenic seed banks to preserve genetic diversity
Designating marine protected areas around coral reefs

questions.explanation: Ex-situ conservation preserves species or genetic material outside their natural habitat. Cryogenic seed banks (e.g., the Svalbard Global Seed Vault) store plant genetic material under controlled conditions and are a textbook ex-situ method. Wildlife sanctuaries, national parks, and marine protected areas all protect species within their natural habitat, making them in-situ conservation approaches — the most common distractor confusion in exams.

questions.stem: The Nicobar Islands, a Union Territory of India, fall within which of the following globally recognized Biodiversity Hotspots?

options.option_text: Western Ghats & Sri Lanka hotspot region
Indo-Burma hotspot covering Southeast Asia
Sundaland hotspot spanning Southeast Asian islands
Eastern Himalayas hotspot of Northeast India

questions.explanation: The Sundaland Hotspot covers the western half of the Indo-Malayan archipelago — Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java, Borneo — and extends northward to include India's Nicobar Islands. Importantly, the Andaman Islands are NOT part of Sundaland. Candidates commonly confuse the Nicobar with Indo-Burma (which covers northeast India) or place both island groups in the same hotspot, making this a precise and frequently tested distinction.

questions.stem: In conservation biology, a species selected for protection specifically because safeguarding its large habitat range simultaneously shields many other co-existing species is called a/an:

options.option_text: Keystone species critical to food-web structure
Umbrella species for multi-species habitat protection
Flagship species used in public awareness campaigns
Indicator species signaling environmental health changes

questions.explanation: An Umbrella Species has a large enough habitat requirement that protecting it automatically conserves habitat for many other species beneath its 'umbrella' — e.g., Tigers in India. The most tempting distractor is Keystone Species, which exerts a disproportionate ecological role relative to its abundance (e.g., sea otters controlling urchin populations) — a different concept. Flagship species are chosen for fundraising/public appeal, not habitat coverage.

questions.stem: The 'Indo-Burma' Biodiversity Hotspot, one of India's four recognized hotspots, primarily encompasses which region within the country?

options.option_text: The Western Ghats forests extending to coastal Karnataka
The northeastern states including Assam, Manipur, and Mizoram
The Deccan Plateau and Eastern Ghats dry forests
The Gangetic Plains and riparian forests of UP and Bihar

questions.explanation: The Indo-Burma Hotspot spans northeastern India (Assam, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Tripura), Bangladesh, Myanmar, and parts of Southeast Asia — making it a transboundary hotspot rich in freshwater turtles and endemic birds. India's four hotspots are: (1) Himalayas, (2) Indo-Burma, (3) Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, (4) Sundaland. Confusing Indo-Burma with the Himalayan hotspot (which covers the northern mountain arc) is the classic error.

questions.stem: To qualify as a Biodiversity Hotspot under Conservation International's criteria, a region must retain no more than what percentage of its original natural vegetation cover?

options.option_text: No more than 40% of original vegetation remaining
No more than 30% of original vegetation remaining
No more than 50% of original vegetation remaining
No more than 20% of original vegetation remaining

questions.explanation: The two strict criteria for a Biodiversity Hotspot are: (1) the region must contain at least 1,500 species of endemic vascular plants (>0.5% of global total), AND (2) it must have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation — meaning it retains no more than 30%. Candidates confuse this with 50% (too lenient) or 20% (too strict). The 30% threshold reflects the 'threatened' dimension of hotspots — high endemism combined with severe habitat loss.

questions.stem: The Nagoya Protocol (2010), adopted under the Convention on Biological Diversity, primarily provides a legal framework for which of the following?

options.option_text: Establishing financial mechanisms for hotspot restoration projects
Regulating international trade in endangered species globally
Ensuring fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources
Setting binding emission targets to reduce biodiversity-threatening warming

questions.explanation: The Nagoya Protocol governs 'Access and Benefit Sharing' (ABS) — ensuring that countries and communities providing genetic resources (e.g., medicinal plant knowledge) receive equitable benefits when those resources are commercially exploited by foreign entities. The most dangerous distractor is Option B: regulating trade in endangered species is the mandate of CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species), not the Nagoya Protocol — a distinction SSC and UPSC papers have tested multiple times.
